sm: The host explains that it is deer season, with millions of hunters filling freezers while nearly one in five American kids are food insecure. Hunters can donate deer to certified processors, who turn the meat into meals for food banks, pantries and school backpack programs. These programs already existed, but President Trump signed an executive order on September seventeenth, titled Reinvigorating America's Hunting Heritage, that boosts them. Section five directs the agriculture secretary to issue guidance on supporting state wild game donation programs. It also directs the interior secretary to use Pittman-Robertson funds, which come from taxes on firearms, ammunition and archery equipment, to cover processing and distribution costs. The host also says venison is leaner than beef and notes that over eleven million Americans hunt and harvest about three hundred million pounds of venison each year.

The host describes Hunters for the Hungry, an NRA-supported national program with a network of certified processors, which he says provides more than eight point one million meals a year, mostly in Virginia, Missouri, Iowa, Pennsylvania and Ohio. He explains that hunters need a license and a tag, can buy extra tags, and many go unfilled, so programs ask hunters to harvest and donate an additional deer. One deer yields about fifty pounds of lean meat, enough for roughly two hundred quarter-pound burgers, and less than three percent of harvested venison is donated. To donate, a hunter finds a participating processor, ideally calls ahead, field dresses the deer and drops it off. A reporter adds that South Carolina Hunters for the Hungry has donated over one and a half million pounds in twenty years, more than six million meals, including one hundred ten thousand venison sticks for school backpack programs.
